options: A planned, scheduled upgrade to the Ethereum protocol
The network replacing a set of previously-accepted blocks with a different set, after two competing chains briefly exist
A user manually reversing their own transaction
A node provider changing which RPC method it supports
questions.explain: A reorg happens when a competing chain wins out over blocks a node had already accepted, discarding those blocks and everything only contained in them.

questions.q: Why can an event your listener already reacted to simply stop being true?
options: Listeners randomly drop a percentage of valid events by design
Events can only be read once per node, so re-reading always fails
Events automatically expire after 24 hours regardless of the chain
If the block containing it gets discarded in a reorg, that event never happened on the winning chain
questions.explain: A reorg can remove the very block an event was in, meaning anything your code already did in response to it was based on a transaction that is no longer part of the canonical chain.

questions.q: What is the standard, most common way backends protect against reorgs?
options: Ignore the first event on every new block by default
Run their own independent blockchain to avoid reorgs entirely
Refuse to process any transaction until the entire chain has reached finality
Treat a transaction or event as final only after it has a certain number of confirmations
questions.explain: Waiting for N confirmations (blocks built on top of the one containing the transaction/event) reduces the odds it will later be reorg'd out, at the cost of latency.

questions.q: What is the direct signal that a reorg happened at a given block height, when tracking block hashes?
options: The block number suddenly skips by more than one
The RPC provider returns an HTTP 500 error
The hash of a block at a height you've already seen changes to a different value
The gas price at that block drops to zero
questions.explain: If the block at a previously-seen height now has a different hash, the chain has been reorganized at that point, and anything processed from there onward needs re-verifying.

questions.q: Why is a higher confirmations count safer but slower?
options: A higher confirmations count directly increases the gas price paid
It has no effect on safety, only on the UI's loading spinner
It only matters for transactions, never for events
More blocks built on top make the original block less likely to be reorg'd out, but you have to wait longer for them to be mined
questions.explain: Each additional confirmation represents another block built on top of the target block, which practically (though not absolutely) decreases reorg risk — at the cost of additional wait time.
